title: CSV Column Counter: Check the Header Shape
description: Count the fields in a CSV header line with the CSV Column Counter — the quick shape check imports demand before you upload. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a store export whose header reads name,lat,lon,address,phone counts 5 columns — and if your import template expects 4, you have just saved a failed upload.
quick_answer: The CSV Column Counter counts the comma-separated fields in the first non-empty line of a pasted CSV snippet — usually the header. Paste the snippet and read the count — the ten-second check that a file matches the column structure an import expects.
steps_intro: Imports fail on shape before content. Check the shape first:

body.t: The template says 6 columns; the file says 7. Find out here, not from the importer’s error log. Rows get the same treatment in the
A supplier swears the format never changes — until the month it does. A header count is the tripwire that catches silent format drift.
On a server console or a locked-down machine with no Excel, a pasted header still answers the only question that matters right now.
Your script emits CSV; the counter verifies the header it actually wrote — quoted commas inside fields included in the caveat below.
‘name,lat,lon’ counts 3 — the minimum viable coordinate file. Add ‘address’ and the count says 4; the number is trivial, and catching its change early is the whole value.
A header ending in a comma (‘name,lat,lon,’) counts a phantom empty fourth field. Importers disagree about that ghost column — the count makes it visible before they argue.

popular_table.note: The counter reads the first non-empty line and splits on commas — a deliberately simple instrument. Quoted fields containing commas need a full CSV parser; the method note on this page says so plainly.

faq: Does it count data rows too?
No — columns live in the header. The CSV Row Counter is the sibling that counts records; together they describe a file’s shape in two numbers.
What if the file has no header?
Then the first non-empty line is data, and the count still describes its field shape — which is often the question (‘how many fields per row?’) anyway.
European Excel loves semicolons. This counter splits on commas as its method states; a semicolon file will count 1, which is itself the diagnosis.
‘"Smith, John",40.7,-74.0’ fools simple splitting (it would count the name as two). For quoted-heavy files, use a real parser — the tool’s simplicity is stated, not hidden.
Different delimiters need different tools; the count of 1 across a pasted TSV is the tell that you are in comma territory with the wrong-shaped file.
Skipped — the first non-empty line is the measured one, matching how importers hunt for headers.
Can it check every row has the same count?
That is full validation — the CSV Coordinate Validator family checks coordinate content; row-shape auditing belongs to spreadsheet or script checks.
